name: Monobenzone

lead: Monobenzone is a topical drug that permanently removes pigment from skin. Its approved use is in people with widespread vitiligo, where it evens out the remaining normal skin to match the depigmented patches.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a permanent skin whitener, with members weighing whether to go paler than their natural tone. Laboratory studies report that tyrosinase in melanocytes converts it into reactive quinones that bind cellular proteins and trigger an immune response against pigmented cells, leading to lasting loss of melanocytes. No trial has tested it for cosmetic lightening of normal skin.

paras: In its approved use it is a prescription cream applied to remaining pigmented skin in extensive vitiligo under medical supervision. Forum threads also describe online and gray-market purchasing for cosmetic use.

Reported effects include irritation, contact dermatitis, allergic reactions and depigmentation at untreated sites. The effect is described as permanent and does not reverse after stopping. It is prescription-only in the US, and use outside vitiligo is off-label.

web.title: Depigmentation Therapies for Vitiligo (Grimes and Nashawati)

angle.text: A prescription cream that destroys pigment cells so skin ends up uniformly pale; approved for extensive vitiligo. Forums discuss it as a permanent whitener, though use outside vitiligo is off-label and the effect is described as irreversible.

lead: Monobenzone, also called monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH) or 4-(benzyloxy)phenol, is a topical depigmenting agent. Its appearance purpose is evening skin tone: in people with extensive vitiligo, whose skin already has large depigmented patches, it removes pigment from the remaining normally coloured skin so that the whole surface matches [1][2][3]. In the United States it is a prescription-only drug, and its effect is described in the literature as irreversible, because it leads to the loss of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells [4][5][3].

Laboratory research has found that monobenzone is converted by tyrosinase inside melanocytes into reactive quinone species that bind to proteins and make pigmented cells a target for the immune system, rather than only blocking pigment production [4][6][7]. A 2017 review proposes calling the resulting condition 'chemical-induced vitiligo', since it looks the same clinically and under the microscope as vitiligo from other causes [3]. The same immune mechanism has been investigated in melanoma, in a small phase 2a trial combining monobenzone with imiquimod [8].

The compound first drew attention in the late 1930s, when workers in a rubber plant developed patchy depigmentation after handling rubber containing it as an antioxidant, according to Grokipedia; the US FDA approved a branded cream for extensive vitiligo in 1952, per the same source [2]. Today the brand is described as no longer marketed in the US, with compounded preparations the main source [2].

In looksmaxxing communities, monobenzone is discussed as a 'permanent skin whitener' and as a product that some members consider using to lighten their overall skin tone, with ordering from online pharmacies and gray-market sellers described in forum threads [9][10]. No published trial has evaluated it as a cosmetic lightener in people without vitiligo, and its depigmentation is not reversible once established [1][2].
infobox: Prescription-only in the US; unscheduled in Canada [1]

paras: The recognised medical use is depigmentation of normally pigmented skin in people whose vitiligo already covers a large share of the body, commonly described as more than half of the body surface area [1][2]. The aim is an even skin tone once repigmentation treatments have failed or are unsuitable [2][3]. A 2017 review in Dermatologic Clinics describes depigmenting the remaining normal skin as an option for extensive vitiligo that does not respond to repigmentation therapy, and says candidates need careful screening and thorough education; it lists monobenzone alongside 4-methoxyphenol and 88 percent phenol as permanent topical agents, with cryotherapy and lasers as physical methods [3]. Clinical guidelines for vitiligo likewise describe depigmentation as an option for extensive disease [11].

Wikipedia's article on vitiligo explains the context: the condition affects an estimated 0.1 to 2.1 percent of people, usually begins in childhood or young adulthood, and can cause distress when patches are visible on the face, hands or arms. Other options for vitiligo include topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, ruxolitinib cream (approved in the US in 2022), narrowband UVB phototherapy, melanocyte transplantation and cosmetic camouflage; depigmentation is described as being for extensive disease, takes about a year, and requires lifelong sun protection [12].
Monobenzone has also been explored in melanoma immunotherapy research, which is a separate research use and not an appearance use [8].

Human research on monobenzone is limited and centres on its use as a depigmenting agent in people with extensive vitiligo. Evidence-based guidelines for vitiligo treatment have described depigmentation as an option for widespread disease [11], and a 1985 report in Archives of Dermatology described dermatitis arising from monobenzone applications in patients with active vitiligo [13].

A 2018 phase 2a trial examined monobenzone combined with imiquimod, applied locally, in 25 patients with stage III-IV melanoma and non-resectable cutaneous metastases (21 evaluable at 12 weeks). It reported partial regression in 8 patients at 12 weeks, clinical responses in 11 with prolonged treatment including 3 complete responses, melanoma-specific immune responses in a share of those tested, and vitiligo-like depigmentation on untreated skin in 7 patients. It concerned cancer immunotherapy rather than cosmetic depigmentation [8].

Most mechanistic work, including studies of tyrosinase haptenation, melanocyte-specific immunity and a mouse model of monobenzone-induced vitiligo, was done in cell and animal systems rather than in clinical trials [4][5][14]. The 2011 study by van den Boorn and colleagues reported that monobenzone binds tyrosinase, causes oxidative stress in melanosomes, and drives release of antigens that activate dendritic cells and prime T cells against melanocytes and melanoma cells, including in animal models [4]. A secondary summary reports that depigmentation was achieved in a large majority of selected patients with severe vitiligo, but it does not rest on a large randomised trial [2].

Reported effects include skin irritation and contact dermatitis, which have been described in people with active vitiligo [13]. Reference text describing the drug also reports allergic reactions and depigmentation at sites distant from where it was applied, including covered skin [2]. Grokipedia lists common local effects such as redness, itching and dryness, possible eye effects, UV sensitivity, and contraindications including hypersensitivity, active skin inflammation or infection, pregnancy (where risk and benefit must be weighed) and young children [2].

The central feature is irreversibility: once melanocytes are lost, pigment does not return, which is why the product label and clinicians treat the decision as permanent and associate the drug with sun-protection needs afterwards [2][12]. Wikipedia's vitiligo article states that lifelong sun protection is needed after depigmentation to prevent severe sunburn [12]. Dermatology guidance also stresses psychological readiness and expectations before treatment [2][3].

Grokipedia says a 2003 label revision added stronger warnings about permanence, sun exposure and risks such as exogenous ochronosis, and that its misuse as an illicit bleaching agent, including for melasma, carries serious risk of permanent and unpredictable depigmentation [2]. Wikipedia's article on skin whitening describes the wider category of bleaching products and their reported health risks, which are mostly associated with other agents such as mercury, hydroquinone and corticosteroids [15].

Monobenzone is a pro-hapten: tyrosinase in melanocytes oxidises it to a reactive ortho-quinone that conjugates with thiols and tyrosinase protein [6][7]. A 2011 study reported that this haptenation, together with melanosome oxidative stress, makes pigmented cells more immunogenic and drives T-cell responses against melanocyte antigens [4]. A 2016 study in mice described a long-lasting, melanocyte-specific response dependent on natural killer cells [5]. A mouse model of vitiligo induced by monobenzone has also been described [14]. A review frames the process as moving from enzymatic blockade to autoimmunity [6].

Wikipedia describes the post-treatment skin as resembling vitiligo, with a normal epidermis but no identifiable melanocytes [1]. Older descriptions emphasised tyrosinase inhibition and increased melanin release from melanocytes; the later immunological work adds that the loss of melanocytes is driven by an immune response, which helps explain depigmentation at distant sites [1][6].

Monobenzone is the monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, with formula C13H12O2 and a molar mass of about 200 g/mol. It is a white to colourless crystalline solid that dissolves in alcohol, benzene and diethyl ether but hardly in water [1][2]. Its ATC code is D11AX13 [1].

Grokipedia traces the compound to 1939, when rubber-plant workers developed patchy depigmentation from an antioxidant containing it, which led to its removal from many industrial formulations; animal studies in the 1940s showed it reduced melanin formation, and clinical work in the 1950s supported its intentional use in extensive vitiligo [2]. A 2017 review notes that chemical-induced depigmentation has been known for more than 75 years, first as an occupational hazard and later through everyday products such as hair dyes [3].

Wikipedia lists monobenzone as prescription-only in the United States and unscheduled in Canada [1]. A brand-name cream, Benoquin, is described in a Grokipedia article as discontinued in the US, with compounded 20% preparations available; the same article says the EU and India restrict or ban it in cosmetics [2].

Threads on looksmax.org include members asking whether monobenzone is worth using to become paler, weighing it against keeping a natural tan [10]. Other threads ask whether any members have tried it as a permanent skin whitener [16]. Some posts describe ordering the cream from overseas online pharmacies, and members also speculate about whether others' appearance reflects skin-lightening products [9][17]. Community discussion often includes commentary about identity and skin colour; this article records only that such discussions exist.

Skin lightening more broadly has a long history and a wide cultural footprint. Wikipedia describes practices recorded since antiquity, usage figures of 25 to 77 percent of women in some African surveys and around 40 percent in parts of Asia, links to social status and colourism, and regulatory bans such as the EU's 2000 ban of hydroquinone in cosmetics [15]. Monobenzone differs from the usual products in that it is a medical drug whose effect is permanent [2][15].

lore.intro: Monobenzone appears in looksmaxxing forums as a permanent skin-whitening option and is often mentioned alongside other lightening products; some posts describe gray-market ordering.[9][10]
